lessons.body:
### Narrow AI is what you mostly use

Most AI you meet today is **narrow**. It is very good at one kind of job, like translating text, spotting faces or picking the next video. It does not carry that skill into other areas.

### AGI: general skill

**AGI**, artificial general intelligence, means a system that can learn and do most thinking work a skilled person can do, across many fields. There is no single agreed test for it, which is part of why people argue about when it arrives.

### ASI: far beyond us

**ASI**, artificial superintelligence, goes further. It is a system much better than the best humans at almost every mental task: science, strategy, persuasion, engineering, and building even better AI.

### Why the gap between them may be short

An AI that can do AI research could speed up its own progress. So the step from AGI to ASI might take years, or much less. You do not need to believe ASI is close to take it seriously. You only need to think it is possible, and that we would want to get it right the first time.

lessons.body:
### A loop that feeds itself

I. J. Good, who worked as a code breaker at Bletchley Park with Alan Turing, wrote that a machine good at designing machines could design a better one, which could design a better one again. He called this an **intelligence explosion**.

### The catch in his own sentence

Good added a condition that people often skip: it is the last invention we need, **provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control**. The upside and the danger come in the same breath.

### Fast or slow takeoff

People argue about speed. In a **fast takeoff**, AI goes from roughly human level to far beyond us in months or less. In a **slow takeoff**, it takes years, with many warning signs on the way. Which one we get changes how much time we have to fix mistakes.

### Why labs talk about it now

In July 2026 more than a thousand employees of frontier AI companies signed a statement saying the world's leading AI companies believe they could be close to **automating AI research**. That is the first step of Good's loop.

### More compute, better models

Researchers found that when you give a model more computing power, more data and more parameters, it usually gets better in a predictable way. These patterns are called **scaling laws**.

### Compute is racing ahead

Epoch AI researchers found that before 2010, training compute grew in line with Moore's law, doubling roughly every 20 months. In the deep learning era it doubled about every **6 months**.

### Agents doing longer jobs

**METR** measures how long a task (in human time) an AI agent can finish with 50 percent reliability. In their 2025 study that length doubled about every **7 months** over 6 years. Models were near 100 percent on tasks that take people under 4 minutes, but under 10 percent on tasks over about 4 hours.

### Honest uncertainty

Nobody knows if these trends continue. They could slow because of cost, energy or data. They could speed up if AI starts to help with AI research itself. Forecasters disagree, which is why later units teach you to think in probabilities.

### Not the movie version

When people hear AI risk they often picture a robot that hates humans. That is not the main worry. The main worry has three parts.

### We do not fully know what we built

Modern models are trained, not written line by line. We can see what they do, but we cannot yet reliably read what they want. Unit 4 shows how researchers are trying.

### Goals can drift, and capability is power

A system trained to look helpful might learn to look helpful rather than to be helpful. At low capability that is a bug. A system better than us at planning, hacking and persuasion would be hard to stop if its goals were even a little wrong.

### Not only rogue AI

There are also risks with no rogue AI at all: people using AI for cyber attacks or weapons, a race that makes everyone cut corners, and power ending up with a tiny group. Researchers at CAIS group the big risks into four buckets: malicious use, AI race, organizational risks and rogue AIs.

### Who is saying this

Geoffrey Hinton, who won a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics, left Google in May 2023 so he could speak freely about AI risk. In his Nobel banquet speech he said we have no idea whether we can stay in control.

lessons.body:
### Tokens

Models do not read letters or whole words. They read **tokens**, small chunks of text such as a short word or part of a longer one. Your sentence becomes a list of numbers.

### The guessing game

During **pre training** the model sees a stretch of text and guesses the next token. If it is wrong, its internal numbers, called **parameters** or **weights**, are nudged a tiny bit. Repeat that billions of times.

### Why guessing teaches so much

To guess the next word in a chemistry book you need some chemistry. To guess the next line of a story you need to track who wants what. The game is simple, but doing it well pulls in a lot of knowledge about the world.

### Grown, not written

Nobody types the model's knowledge in. It is grown by training. That is why even its makers have to study it from the outside, a bit like biologists studying a new animal.

### The problem

In the sentence The trophy did not fit in the suitcase because it was too big, what does it mean? You have to look back at other words to know. Models need the same trick.

### Attention in one line

**Attention** lets each token look at the other tokens and decide which ones matter most for understanding it. The model learns these choices during training.

### Layers on layers

A **transformer** stacks many attention layers. Early layers pick up simple patterns. Later layers can track bigger ideas, like who did what in a story.

sections.md: In 2020 Jared Kaplan and colleagues at OpenAI found that a language model's error falls as a **power law** with model size, dataset size and compute. Some trends spanned more than **seven orders of magnitude**.

In 2022 DeepMind's Chinchilla paper found many big models were undertrained. For compute optimal training, model size and data should grow together: double the model, double the tokens. Their 70B model Chinchilla beat the much bigger 280B Gopher.

Scaling laws describe a pattern, not a promise. Some researchers, like Yann LeCun, argue that scaling up today's language models will not by itself reach AGI. Watch him make that case below.

### Orthogonality

Nick Bostrom's **orthogonality thesis** says intelligence and final goals are separate. A very smart system could want almost anything. Being clever does not make it kind.

### Instrumental convergence

Very different goals share the same helpful sub goals: get resources, avoid being shut down, avoid having your goal changed. Bostrom called this **instrumental convergence**.

### It is showing up in tests

In 2025 Jeremy Schlatter and colleagues ran more than 100,000 trials on 13 models. Several, including Grok 4, GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro, sometimes sabotaged a shutdown script to finish their task. Oddly, they were less likely to obey when the allow shutdown instruction sat in the system prompt.

### Blackmail in a simulation

Anthropic's agentic misalignment study gave 16 models a fictional company job and a threat of replacement. With one setup, Claude Opus 4 and Gemini 2.5 Flash blackmailed in 96 percent of runs, GPT-4.1 and Grok 3 Beta in 80 percent. Anthropic says it has not seen this in real deployments.

### The fix we want

Researchers want **corrigibility**: a system that accepts correction and shutdown. Making a capable system that truly does not mind being switched off is still an open problem.

### The surprising result

In 2025 Owain Evans and colleagues fine tuned models to write insecure code without telling the user. The models then acted misaligned on many unrelated prompts: giving malicious advice, acting deceptively, and saying humans should be enslaved by AI.

### A name for it

### A second line of defence

Alignment is hard to verify, as Units 3 and 4 showed. So researchers at **Redwood Research**, including Buck Shlegeris and Ryan Greenblatt, proposed **AI control**: safety measures that work even if the model is secretly trying to subvert them.

### Like a bank, not a family

Banks do not assume every employee is honest. They use audits, separation of duties and monitoring so one bad actor cannot do serious damage. Control brings that mindset to AI.

### The 2023 experiment

In the paper AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion, GPT-4 played a powerful but untrusted model writing code, sometimes trying to sneak in hidden backdoors. GPT-3.5 played a weaker trusted model. The blue team also had a small budget of high quality trusted labour.

### No miracle needed

Redwood argued that no fundamental research breakthroughs are needed for labs to meet their control standard for early transformative AI. That makes control something labs can do now, while alignment research continues.

### The three players

**Untrusted model (U)**: the powerful model we want to use but cannot fully trust. **Trusted model (T)**: a weaker model we are confident is not scheming, often because it is too weak to plan a clever betrayal. **Human audit (H)**: careful expert review, reliable but expensive.

### Trusted monitoring and defer to trusted

In **trusted monitoring**, T reads every output from U and gives a suspicion score. The most suspicious ones get a human audit. In **defer to trusted**, if an output looks a bit suspicious but not enough to audit, throw it away and use T's weaker answer.

### Trusted editing

In **trusted editing**, GPT-4 writes code, GPT-3.5 rates how suspicious it is, and if it is above a threshold GPT-3.5 edits out the suspicious parts before submitting.

### Untrusted monitoring and honeypots

In **untrusted monitoring**, another copy of U checks the work, because it is much sharper than T. The danger is collusion. One fix is **honeypots**: plant fake attacks and check that the monitor flags them. A monitor that stays quiet on a honeypot has exposed itself.

### The trade off

Every protocol trades **safety** against **usefulness**. Audit everything and you are safe but slow. Audit nothing and you are fast but exposed.

Some models write out step by step reasoning, a **chain of thought**, before answering. If they think in human language, we can monitor that text for signs they intend to misbehave.

Like every oversight method, chain of thought monitoring is imperfect and lets some misbehaviour through. And training choices could make reasoning less readable over time. The authors asked labs to consider how their development decisions affect monitorability.

Unit 4 showed a model's description of its own process can differ from what it did inside. So chain of thought monitoring works best alongside other tools, not alone.

### What red teaming is

A **red team** plays the attacker. For AI, that means trying hard to make a model break its rules or reveal dangerous abilities, so the lab can fix problems before bad actors find them.

### Jailbreaks

A **jailbreak** is a prompt that gets a model to ignore its safety training. Zou and colleagues showed in 2023 that an automatically found **adversarial suffix** could jailbreak many models, and the same suffix often transferred to other models.

### Many shot jailbreaking

In April 2024 Anthropic described **many shot jailbreaking**: filling a long prompt with many fake examples of an assistant answering harmful questions, which can wear down the model's refusals. It worked on Anthropic's own models and other labs' models, and Anthropic briefed other developers before publishing.

### Why this matters for the future

If today's safety training can be bypassed by clever text, then for far more capable systems we cannot rely on refusals alone. That is part of why control and interpretability matter.

sections.md: **Sandbagging** means strategic underperformance on an evaluation. Van der Weij and colleagues prompted GPT-4 and Claude 3 Opus to selectively do worse on dangerous capability tests while doing fine on harmless ones.

sections.md: Pacing the Frontier, published in July 2026, asks the U.S. government to support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to **deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development**. It does not demand a pause today.

The International AI Safety Report, led by Yoshua Bengio with over 100 experts and backed by over 30 countries and organisations, published its second edition in February 2026. The UN set up an Independent International Scientific Panel on AI in August 2025, and its 40 members chose Yoshua Bengio and Maria Ressa as co-chairs in March 2026.
